papers.title: OsMED25-OsWRI1 Fine-Tunes Fatty Acid Biosynthesis: A Key Strategy via Intron Retention
papers.abstract: Abstract In rice grains, the mechanisms governing fatty acid biosynthesis remain largely elusive. Although WRINKLED1 (WRI1) is well established as a core transcription factor activating fatty acid biosynthesis under multi-level regulation, its post-transcriptional regulation has been scarcely explored. Here, we demonstrate that OsWRI1 transcripts undergo alternative splicing (AS) via intron retention (IR), producing two functionally distinct splice variants: OsWRI1α and OsWRI1β. OsWRI1α encodes a canonical protein containing two AP2 domains, whereas OsWRI1β produces a truncated protein due to a premature termination codon. Genetic analyses confirm that OsWRI1α functions as a positive regulator of fatty acid biosynthesis, while OsWRI1β exerts an inhibitory effect by directly interacting with OsWRI1α, disrupting its dimerization, and preventing activation of downstream target genes including OsACP1 and OsFAD2. We further identify OsMED25 as a critical regulator of this AS event. OsMED25 is recruited to a 360-bp intronic region of OsWRI1 that corresponds precisely to the retained intron in OsWRI1β, where it recruits the splicing factor OsPTB4 to promote intron retention, thereby repressing fatty acid biosynthesis. The induction of OsWRI1β expression by jasmonic acid (JA) signaling, which we identify as a suppressor of fatty acid biosynthesis, is strictly dependent on OsMED25. Mechanistically, JA enhances OsMED25 protein stability and promotes its association with OsWRI1 pre-mRNA. Together, these findings establish that IR-mediated AS of OsWRI1 defines a regulatory mechanism where the JA-OsMED25-OsPTB4-OsWRI1 axis coordinates carbon flux and energy homeostasis during grain lipid accumulation. Thus, OsMED25 integrates upstream JA signaling to fine-tune OsWRI1 splicing, modulating fatty acid biosynthesis during rice grain development.

papers.title: Phototropin-mediated blue light signaling orients the asymmetry of Marchantia polymorpha spores
papers.abstract: Multicellular organisms produced by sexual reproduction develop from single cells, and the asymmetry of these cells can define the orientation of the earliest developmental axes. The haploid multicellular stage of the plant, Marchantia polymorpha, develops from a single cell—the spore—that divides asymmetrically, producing an apical germ cell that generates the plant body and a smaller basal cell that differentiates as an anchoring germ rhizoid cell. We show that the orientation of this asymmetric cell division is controlled by an external environmental cue—blue light—that is perceived by the photoreceptor phototropin. This process requires the NCH1 (NRL PROTEIN FOR CHLOROPLAST MOVEMENT 1) protein for downstream signaling. Together, these findings define core elements of the mechanism by which a directional environmental signal orients cell division, which, in turn, orients the first axis of symmetry.

papers.title: Developmental Rewiring of a Brassinosteroid Signaling Module Controls Anther Patterning and Tapetum Specification in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: Abstract Male reproductive development in plants relies on the precise patterning of anther locules and the specification of the tapetum layer. While the BRASSINAZOLE RESISTANT (BZR) family transcription factors are essential for both processes, they function independently of the brassinosteroid (BR) receptors, leaving their upstream signaling mechanism unknown. Here, through systematic genetic analysis, we show that a core BR-signaling module, comprising BR-SIGNALING KINASEs (BSKs) and BRASSINOSTEROID-INSENSITIVE 2 (BIN2), is repurposed downstream of the tapetum regulator the receptor kinase EXCESS MICROSPOROCYTES1 (EMS1) and functions upstream of BZRs. Within this reconfigured pathway, EMS1 recruits BSKs, which in turn inactivate BIN2, thereby releasing BZRs in a conserved hierarchy cascade mirroring BR signaling to drive tapetum specification. Additionally, this BSKs-BIN2-BZRs signaling module also functions in anther locule formation. Conversely, BSU1-LIKE2/3 (BSL2/3), homologs of the positive BR regulator BSU1, act as repressors in this context. This pathway transcriptionally activates the cyclins such as CYCB1;1 to initiate tapetal cell division, while BSL2/3 ensure its timely termination by promoting CYCB1;1 protein degradation. Our work defines the signaling framework governing anther development and establishes a paradigm in which conserved signaling components are rewired to achieve developmental specificity.

papers.title: ABI1/ABI2-mediated dephosphorylation of NRAMP1 couples ABA signaling to manganese homeostasis
papers.abstract: Abstract Manganese (Mn) homeostasis, the precise regulation of cellular Mn levels, is crucial for plant growth and is maintained primarily through the transporter NATURAL RESISTANCE-ASSOCIATED MACROPHAGE PROTEIN 1 (NRAMP1). While the kinases responsible for its phosphorylation are well-established, the phosphatases mediating its dephosphorylation remain unidentified. We identify ABI1 and ABI2 as the phosphatases acting on NRAMP1, linking ABA signaling to Mn homeostasis. Mn stresses trigger ABA to inhibit ABI1/2, which may enable NRAMP1 phosphorylation and stress initiation. A feedback loop then appears to induce short-term ABI1/2 reactivation, mediating site-specific dephosphorylation of NRAMP1 at Thr498 (to fine-tune uptake under deficiency) and at Ser20 (to limit endocytosis under toxicity). This dephosphorylation restrains overactivation and contributes to the maintenance of Mn ion balance. Subsequent ABI1/2 attenuation may facilitates long-term adaptation. Collectively, our findings support the ABA-ABI1/2-NRAMP1 axis as a feedback-regulated circuit controlling Mn homeostasis; this work reveals an expanded functional repertoire for ABA-signaling PP2Cs and identifies a targetable module for enhancing crop resilience to Mn stress.

papers.title: The ZmJAZ14–ZmMYC2 module regulates anthesis–silking synchrony in maize
papers.abstract: The evolution of traits can increase yield potential but may create physiological constraints. Jasmonic acid (JA) signaling regulates sex determination in male (tassel) and female (ear) inflorescences in maize. Although the formation of ears laid the foundation for high yields, the asynchronous development of the tassel and the ear prolongs the anthesis-silking interval (ASI), threatening reproductive success and reducing yield. Whether JA signaling coordinates ear and tassel development remains unclear. Here, we show that the core JA signaling module, ZmJAZ14-ZmMYC2a/b, orchestrates the expression of SPL29 for reproductive transition, BA1 for female inflorescence initiation, and EXPA5 for silk elongation. Coordination of these physiological processes underpins synchronous growth of the tassel and ears, whereas disruption of ZmMYC2a/b or accumulation of the repressor ZmJAZ14 prolongs ASI. Our work suggests that the repurposing of JA signaling to coordinate ear and tassel development may represent a lineage-specific evolutionary burden in maize. Deciphering the link between gains and unforeseen costs of evolution could further improve yields.

papers.title: The transcription factors OsIDD and OsSHR jointly regulate ground tissue patterning and differentiation in rice roots
papers.abstract: Rice roots have a distinctive ground tissue architecture with multiple cortical layers and a single endodermal layer concentrically surrounding the stele. This architecture promotes aerenchyma formation and adaptability to waterlogged environments, but the underlying molecular mechanisms remain largely unexplored. Here, we identified the INDETERMINATE DOMAIN (IDD) and SHORTROOT (SHR) families as key regulators of ground tissue development in rice. OsIDD2/3/6/8 govern cortical radial symmetry by coordinating cortical organization and auxin distribution independently of OsSHR1/2/3/4/5. Quadruple knockout of OsIDD2/3/6/8 caused cortical asymmetry without affecting apoplastic barrier integrity or mineral uptake but reduced shoot-directed ion transport. OsIDD8 also controls the number of cortical cell layers and endodermal cells, whereas OsSHR1/2/3/4/5 redundantly promote periclinal divisions of the cortical cells, which require OsIDD8 activity. Moreover, OsIDD and OsSHR members coordinate endodermal differentiation by regulating localization of Casparian strip membrane domain protein OsCASP1 and lignin/suberin deposition. These findings establish a genetic framework underlying the spatial organization and functional differentiation of ground tissue in rice roots.

papers.title: HDAC1/2 mediates the chloroplast unfolded protein response through histone H4 deacetylation in Chlamydomonas
papers.abstract: Abstract Disruption of chloroplast proteostasis activates retrograde signaling that reprograms nuclear gene expression. However, how these signals are integrated with chromatin-based transcriptional regulation remains poorly understood. Here, using a genetic suppressor screen of a conditional ClpP1-depletion mutant, we identified a histone deacetylase HDAC1/2 as a regulator of chloroplast stress signaling in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. Loss of HDAC1/2 alleviated growth inhibition and reduced cell death caused by disruption of chloroplast proteostasis following ClpP1 depletion. Furthermore, HDAC1/2 deficiency enhanced tolerance to high-light, oxidative, and endoplasmic reticulum stresses, as well as chloroplast translation inhibition. These stress conditions increased H2O2 levels and HDAC1/2 protein accumulation, suggesting that H2O2 may act as a common upstream signal. Additionally, HDAC1/2 deficiency also disrupted the transcriptional response to ClpP1 depletion, particularly affecting genes involved in photosynthesis, redox homeostasis, DNA metabolism, cell-cycle regulation, and ROS scavenging. This altered response was accompanied by increased histone H4 acetylation. Together, our findings identify HDAC1/2 as an important regulator connecting organellar proteostasis signaling with nuclear epigenetic regulation and suggest a role for H2O2 associated chromatin remodeling in coordinating cellular stress responses.

Latitude modulates climate-driven maize yield gains across the central U.S. “warming hole”
papers.abstract: Abstract Maize yield responses to climate change differ seasonally and regionally, with both positive and negative impacts shaped by local climate trends and management decisions. Here, using a phenology-aligned moving crop-season framework and the Hybrid-Maize model (1991–2024) across five U.S. Corn Belt states, we quantify climate-driven yield contributions and show that they transition from southern declines to northern gains, reflecting the persistent influence of the central U.S. summer warming hole characterized by cooling maximum temperatures and increasing rainfall. A systematic thermal mismatch between environmental heat availability and hybrid growing degree day requirements is observed, particularly south of 42°N, where thermal matching declined despite favorable thermal conditions. Contrasting trends in thermal matching and reproductive duration help explain the latitude-dependent structure of climate-driven yield contributions. Our findings highlight how hybrid selection modulates the impacts of temperature, precipitation, vapor pressure deficit, and radiation trends on maize yield gains across the U.S. Corn Belt.

papers.title: Cell lineages of soybean anther morphogenesis reveal developmental trajectory of microsporocytes at single-cell resolution
papers.abstract: Abstract In flowering plants, anther morphogenesis and microspore mother cell (MMC) specification of the male reproductive organ are critical for fertility and seed-setting or yield, but their underlying mechanisms in soybean (Glycine max) remain largely uncharacterized. Here, we cytologically established a staged developmental framework of early soybean anthers that were collected to generate a high-resolution single-nucleus RNA-seq atlas. We further characterized 11 major cell types annotated by cluster-specific marker genes and validated by RNA in situ hybridization. Pseudotime trajectory analysis reconstructed the differentiation process of microsporocytes, tapetum, and middle layer from archesporial cells, and established a regulatory network governing germline development. Parallel comparison of mitotic dividing cells (DCs) and meiotic MMCs revealed divergent transcriptional and cell-cycle programs. DCs follow a linear mitotic cascade with smooth, continuous transcriptional regulation, whereas MMCs undergo lineage-specific transcriptional reprogramming with an oscillatory activation of cell-cycle regulators to orchestrate meiotic transitions and progression. By comparing the transcriptional regulatory network of DCs and MMCs, we identified a pair of C2H2 zinc finger factors GmKNUa/b, the homologs of Arabidopsis KNUCKLES, as a key switch for MMC differentiation in soybean. The CRISPR-Cas9-edited Gmknua/b double mutants lack meiocytes, and GmKNUa/b might trigger the mitosis-to-meiosis transition by repressing the persistent mitotic cell cycle. Taken together, these results reveal the cellular signatures and molecular basis of early soybean anther morphogenesis and germline specialization, and provide candidate targets for manipulating germline fate and male fertility in soybean.

papers.title: PHYTOCHROME INTERACTING FACTOR 7 moderates the activity of phytochrome A in persistent canopy shade conditions
papers.abstract: In nature, plants perceive and respond to complex vegetative environments through the phytochrome (phy) photoreceptor-signaling system. The Canopy Adaptation Strategy, elicited by phyA, together with the Shade Avoidance Syndrome, regulated by phyB, enables plants to adapt to diverse forms of vegetation shade. The phyA High Irradiance Response mode, which involves photocycle-coupled nuclear shuttling, is essential for sensing sustained far-red-rich conditions typical of canopy or occlusive shade. Our research identifies PHYTOCHROME INTERACTING FACTOR 7 (PIF7) as a key regulator of phyA function. We show that PIF7 overexpression (PIF7ox) effectively suppresses phyA action. Under persistent shade, PIF7 and phyA both accumulate and associate within nuclear photobodies, with this interaction mediated by the C-terminal domain of PIF7 and the PAS-PAS domain of phyA. PIF7 also interacts with FAR-RED ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL 1 (FHY1) and FHY1-LIKE transport facilitators, thereby interfering with phyA cytosolic-nuclear shuttling. This coordinated molecular targeting by PIF7 constitutes an effective strategy for modulating phyA function under persistent shade conditions.
papers.affiliation: Institute of Molecular Plant Sciences, School of Biological Sciences, University of Edinburgh

papers.title: The E3 ubiquitin ligase CRL4DDRM3 targets CDT1 for degradation to facilitate homologous recombination in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: Abstract DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) are considered the most cytotoxic form of DNA damage. Homologous recombination (HR) is an accurate DSB repair pathway. However, the regulatory mechanisms of HR are still poorly understood in plants. The DNA replication licensing factor CDC10-dependent transcript 1 (CDT1) is highly conserved in eukaryotes. The human CDT1 is subjected to polyubiquitination and degradation mediated by the E3 ubiquitin ligases CRL4CDT2 and SCFSKP2, ensuring that DNA replicates only once per cell cycle. But the E3 ubiquitin ligase(s) targeting plant CDT1 has not been firmly identified yet. Here we show that a previously uncharacterized WD40 protein DNA Damage Response Mutant 3 (DDRM3)/Hypersensitive to Zebularine 11 (HZE11), facilitates HR in Arabidopsis. The ddrm3 mutants show reduced HR efficiency and are thus hypersensitive to multiple DSB-inducing agents. Biochemical analysis reveals that DDRM3 directly interacts with DDB1 to form the E3 ubiquitin ligase CRL4DDRM3, which mediates the polyubiquitination and degradation of CDT1. Genetically, silencing CDT1 partially rescues the hypersensitivity of ddrm3 to DSB-inducing agents. Interestingly, overexpression of CDT1 reduces HR efficiency. Altogether, these data suggest that DDRM3 facilitates HR by targeting CDT1 for degradation.

papers.title: A pathogen-induced UGT genomic locus contributes to sinapic acid glycosylation and gray blight resistance in tea plant
papers.abstract: Abstract UDP-glycosyltransferases (UGTs) are a superfamily essential for plant ecological adaptation, catalyzing the conversion of secondary metabolites into diverse bioactive glycosides. However, how UGTs efficiently modulate glycoside biosynthesis in response to environmental stresses remains unclear. Here, we characterized a pathogen-induced UGT genomic locus in the tea plant (Camellia sinensis) that responds to gray blight infection. Functional analyses showed that CsUGT84A22 converted sinapic acid into the antifungal compound sinapoyl-β-D-glucose (S-G). Suppression of CsUGT84A22 reduced S-G accumulation and impaired gray blight resistance in tea plants. In addition, CsMYB73, a transcription factor encoded within the genomic locus, negatively regulated CsUGT84A22 expression, and suppression of CsMYB73 enhanced both gray blight resistance and S-G biosynthesis. Furthermore, jasmonic acid (JA) biosynthesis was stimulated to improve gray blight resistance with accelerating CsUGT84A22 expression and S-G accumulation. Co-expression network analysis revealed that the JA signaling repressor CsJAZ14 negatively regulates gray blight resistance; specifically, in the absence of JA, it facilitates the CsMYB73-mediated suppression of CsUGT84A22 expression. Evolutionary trajectory analysis further indicated that the genomic locus was fully assembled from grasses to rosids, but diverged within the fabid lineage with loss of MYB73 homology. Together, these findings support a regulatory model in which JA signaling modulates a pathogen-induced genomic locus to promote disease resistance and provide a tractable route for engineering biosynthesis of natural antifungal compounds.

papers.title: OsCPK17- and OsMPK6-mediated dual phosphorylation of OsPUB12 maintains OsPUB2-regulated OsPUB12 homeostasis and balances rice immunity
Auxin-dependent miR167-ARF6/8.1-SAURs module coordinates local growth to shape floret diversification in Asteraceae
papers.abstract: Abstract The corolla is a primary determinant of floral architecture and reproductive success. However, the processes that translate localized growth patterns into species-specific morphologies remain unclear. The complex inflorescences (capitula) of Asteraceae consist of different types of flowers. In Chrysanthemum × morifolium, anemone-type varieties represent a distinct floral form characterized by dramatically elongated corolla tubes in bisexual disc florets. Using the anemone-type chrysanthemum, characterized by dramatically elongated disc florets, we demonstrate that sustained corolla formation depends on localized auxin enrichment. Two auxin response factors, CmARF6 and CmARF8.1, have been identified as positive regulators of this process. These ARFs are post-transcriptionally regulated by miR167 in a dose-dependent manner, establishing a regulatory module that directly activates the auxin-biosynthesis gene CmYUC2 and auxin-transport gene CmPILS1. Concurrently, CmARF6 and CmARF8.1 stimulate localized tissue proliferation by activating CmSAUR64 and CmSAUR76. Comparative analyses across diverse Asteraceae species suggest that auxin-associated regulatory mechanisms may contribute to region-specific corolla growth. Our findings demonstrate that auxin regulation contributes to region-specific corolla growth in the bisexual disc florets of chrysanthemum, providing a framework for investigating related morphological variation in other Asteraceae species.
papers.affiliation: Beijing Key Laboratory of Ornamental Plants Germplasm Innovation & Molecular Breeding

papers.title: VAMP725 and VAMP726 interact with cellulose synthase to support secondary cell wall formation
papers.abstract: The formation of plant cell walls underpins morphogenesis, growth, and development of all plants. Cellulose is an essential and load-bearing cell wall polymer that is synthesized by Cellulose Synthase (CESA) protein complexes at the plasma membrane. In this study, we reveal that SNARE proteins Vesicle Associated Membrane Protein 726 (VAMP726) and VAMP725 associate with multiple CESA proteins. Consistent with these results, the VAMP726 is codelivered with the CESA proteins to the plasma membrane, and the proteins colocalize at intracellular compartments. We further show that the VAMPs, especially VAMP726, are important for CESA trafficking and sustenance of cellulose synthesis both in growing tissues and in secondary wall producing maturing tissues. Taken together, our study outlines an important intracellular process whereby VAMP proteins facilitate trafficking of CESA complexes during cellulose synthesis.

papers.title: A heavy molybdenum reservoir in Neoarchean seawater tracks extensive iron oxidation
papers.abstract: The lead-up to the Great Oxidation Event (GOE; between 2.5 and 2.2 Ga) was arguably as consequential as the event itself, yet substantial uncertainties remain regarding the timing and magnitude of oxygen rise in early Earth’s oceans. Heavy molybdenum isotope compositions (δ 98 Mo) in Neoarchean marine sediments have traditionally been interpreted as evidence for adsorption of dissolved Mo onto iron oxyhydroxides [e.g., ferrihydrite; Fe(OH) 3 ] and manganese oxides (MnO 2 ) formed in oxygenated marine environments, implying at least regional surface oxygen accumulation immediately prior to the GOE. Here, we propose an alternate explanation in which these isotopic signatures arose in a largely anoxic ocean. Analyses of Neoarchean banded iron formations (BIFs) deposited at 2.57 to 2.51 Ga reveal a broad range of δ 98 Mo values, which are best explained by the combined effects of Mo adsorption onto primary ferrihydrite, followed by its diagenetic incorporation into Fe(II)-Mo(IV)-sulfides. After accounting for isotopic fractionation during adsorption, we estimate that Neoarchean seawater δ 98 Mo maintained a relatively stable composition between 1.5‰ and 1.6‰. A newly developed Mo isotope mass balance model further indicates that only a minor MnO 2 sink was required to generate these heavy δ 98 Mo values. Instead, the dominant control was likely removal of isotopically light Mo via adsorption to settling ferrihydrite particles in ferruginous seawater. Given the lack of oxygen indicators for cyanobacterial photosynthesis, we posit that anoxygenic photosynthetic bacteria (photoferrotrophs) were the primary drivers of ferrihydrite precipitation during BIF deposition. Together, these findings imply that the Neoarchean Mo isotope record reflects anaerobic biological oxidation of Fe(II) rather than pervasive surface seawater oxygenation preceding the GOE.
papers.affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Lithospheric and Environmental Coevolution, Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences

papers.title: A SNP in the MdWRKY11 promoter controls the segregation of Glomerella leaf blotch susceptibility in apple
papers.abstract: Abstract Glomerella leaf blotch (GLB), a severe fungal disease caused by Colletotrichum gloeosporioides, threatens the apple (Malus domestica Borkh.) industry worldwide. The susceptibility of apple to GLB is controlled by a single dominant locus. Although several markers for GLB susceptibility have been developed, the causal genes and their functional variations have not been explored. In this study, we used MapQTL and fine mapping to identify SNP544 C/G in the MdWRKY11 promoter as the major factor underlying the variation in GLB susceptibility in apple. The SNP544 G allele generates a W-box motif that is directly bound by MdWRKY29 and activates MdWRKY11 expression during C. gloeosporioides infection. In turn, MdWRKY11 binds to the MdDMR6.1 promoter and activates its expression, leading to salicylic acid degradation and leaf necrosis. The MdWRKY11 SNP544 G allele was strongly associated with GLB susceptibility, with a prediction accuracy of 96.2% in 767 Malus accessions. In addition to SNP544, we identified nine allelic variations in MdWRKY11 across 29 Malus accessions, with a combined prediction accuracy for GLB susceptibility of 99.6%. These findings shed light on the genetic control of GLB susceptibility in apple and provide an efficient molecular marker for breeding GLB-resistant cultivars.
papers.affiliation: College of Horticulture, China Agricultural University , Beijing 100193 ,

papers.title: Leaf hydraulic and photosynthetic traits mediate forest-scale resource use efficiencies across the continental United States
papers.abstract: Temperate forests play a critical role in global carbon cycling and other ecosystem services, yet their resilience to climatic stresses remains uncertain. We combined physiology, community composition, flux data, and modeling to test a functional trait-based approach to predict forest ecosystem processes. For eight U.S. forests spanning broad precipitation and temperature gradients, we scaled up key leaf functional traits—maximum carboxylation velocity of Rubisco ( V c , m a x ), maximum leaf hydraulic conductance ( K l , m a x ), and turgor loss point (that is, wilting point, π t l p ) to predict gross primary productivity, light-use efficiency, standard and intrinsic water-use efficiency (WUE and iWUE), and their sensitivities to soil drought. In multiple regressions, ecosystem processes were strongly associated with community-weighted mean (CWM) trait values: enhanced productivity was linked with high V c , m a x ¯ , K l , m a x ¯ and π t l p ¯ , whereas high WUE and iWUE were linked with low K l , m a x ¯ and high π t l p ¯ . The CWM functional traits also influenced the sensitivity of ecosystem processes to soil moisture. A causal role of functional traits in driving ecosystem processes alongside climate was supported by parameterizing the LM4.1 vegetation model with CWM functional traits. This study highlights the important role of functional traits in determining forest responses to climate-driven water stress at a continental scale.
papers.affiliation: High Meadows Environmental Institute, Princeton University

papers.title: Effector-triggered stomatal immunity prevents leaf invasion by bacterial pathogens
papers.abstract: The phytopathogen Pseudomonas syringae must enter the leaf interior through natural openings such as stomata to cause disease. Plants restrict pathogen entry into the leaf through non–self-recognition–driven stomatal closure. P. syringae counters this stomatal immunity by deploying a range of toxins and effectors. Here, we show that stomatal immunity in Arabidopsis thaliana is reinforced upon recognition of the ubiquitous P. syringae type III effector AvrE1 by the resistance protein CAR1. CAR1 expression is enriched in guard cells, and its activation prolongs the effective duration of stomatal immunity. We also show that CAR1 prevents the invasion of leaf tissue by natural isolates of P. syringae , demonstrating that stomatal immunity provides a broadly significant barrier to host accessibility by P. syringae that carry the conserved effector AvrE1.
papers.affiliation: Department of Cell and Systems Biology, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON M5S 3G5, Canada.

papers.title: Medicinal plants, lessons from mushrooms and the power of smell: Books in brief
Pre-bilaterian roots of the chordate body plan
Strigolactone receptor D14 integrates phosphate and strigolactone signaling by interacting with and stabilizing PHR1
papers.abstract: Strigolactone (SL) and low phosphate (LP) signaling coordinately regulate shoot and root architecture and plant adaptation. While LP signaling is generally considered upstream of SL biosynthesis, their interaction is more complex. For instance, exogenous SL exerts opposite effects on lateral root formation under low versus high phosphorus. Here, we show that under LP, SL-induced anthocyanin accumulation requires PHR1, demonstrating that PHR1 functions downstream of SL signaling. We uncovered an SL-dependent physical interaction between PHR1 and the SL receptor DWARF14 (D14). This interaction promotes PHR1 dimerization, stabilizes PHR1 by inhibiting its ubiquitination-mediated degradation, and enhances its transcriptional activation activity. The D14-PHR1 complex directly binds and up-regulates the SL biosynthesis gene MAX3 and anthocyanin biosynthesis genes, thereby inhibiting branching and hypocotyl elongation and promoting anthocyanin accumulation. These findings indicate that PHR1 mediates the coordination of SL and LP signaling, potentially explaining SL’s opposing effects on lateral root formation under different phosphorus conditions. In the phr1 mutant, exogenous SL inhibited lateral roots under both LP and Pi-sufficient conditions, confirming that the promoting role of SL under LP requires PHR1. PHR1 also interacted with D14 to activate LBDs and HB23 , regulating lateral root formation. Collectively, LP signaling coordinates with SL signaling via two parallel pathways: regulating SL biosynthesis to align SL functions with LP requirements and enhancing PHR1 activity through PHR1-D14 interaction to amplify LP signaling outputs.
papers.affiliation: State Key Laboratory of Chemo and Biosensing, Hunan Provincial Key Laboratory of Plant Functional Genomics and Developmental Regulation, College of Biology, Longping Agricultural College, Hunan University, Changsha 410082, China.

papers.title: Explainable AI identifies recombination and chromatin environment as key predictors of subgenome evolution in maize and Brassica
papers.abstract: Polyploidy, or whole genome duplication, reshapes genomes through biased gene loss and regulatory rewiring, yet the drivers of biased fractionation among subgenomes remain unclear. Using maize and Brassica rapa as model allopolyploids, we compiled 60 genomic and epigenomic features in maize and 45 in B. rapa and constructed supervised machine learning models to classify genes by subgenome identity. In both species, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approaches identified recombination rate as the most influential and highly interconnected feature despite nonsignificant mean differences between subgenome groups. Chromosome location, transposon density, and chromatin-associated features, including the proximity of accessible chromatin regions to genes and active histone marks such as H3K9ac and H3K27ac, consistently ranked among the top contributors to subgenome classification. XAI-derived covariation and interaction networks further revealed recombination rate as the central node connecting significant features. Together, these results highlight recombination and chromatin environment as major predictors of subgenome divergence in polyploid genomes.
papers.affiliation: Department of Microbiology and Cell Science, Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences, University of Florida, Gainesville, FL 32611, USA.
